title: Organisation and Enzymes
seo_title: Year 10 Science: Organisation and Enzymes Worksheets (GCSE Combined Science)
standard_text: Levels of organisation within a multicellular organism; the digestive system and the role of enzymes (carbohydrases, proteases, lipases) and bile, the lock and key model and the effect of temperature and pH; food tests; the heart, blood vessels and blood; coronary heart disease and its treatment; plant tissues and organs, transpiration and translocation.
meta_desc: Free Year 10 GCSE Combined Science worksheets on organisation: enzymes and the lock and key model, food tests, the heart, blood vessels, blood, coronary heart disease and plant transport. 100 questions with answers.
key_sub: Each enzyme has an optimum temperature and pH; the active site fits one substrate.
body_html:
How to think about it

Cells form tissues, tissues form organs, organs form organ systems.

  • Enzymes are biological catalysts with an active site. High temperatures or the wrong pH change its shape: the enzyme is denatured.
  • The heart pumps blood: arteries carry it away, veins bring it back, capillaries exchange substances.
  • In plants, xylem carries water up (transpiration) and phloem carries sugars (translocation).
Example

Rate highest at 37 °C. Optimum?

The peak

Answer: 37 °C

Example

Test for protein?

Biuret: blue to purple

Answer: biuret reagent

Common mistakes

  • Saying enzymes are killed by heat.
  • Thinking arteries carry blood to the heart.
  • Thinking bile is an enzyme.

faq.q: Why do enzymes stop working at high temperatures?
faq.a: The bonds holding the protein's shape break, so the active site changes shape and the substrate no longer fits. The enzyme is denatured.
Iodine for starch (blue-black), Benedict's solution heated for sugars (brick-red), biuret for protein (purple), and the ethanol emulsion test for lipids (cloudy).

faq.q: What is the difference between arteries, veins and capillaries?
faq.a: Arteries carry blood away from the heart at high pressure; veins carry it back and have valves; capillaries are one cell thick for exchange.
